p.x:
Last Friday evening, Mai was on a crowded bus in Bangkok. She was tired and was looking at her phone. Suddenly, a man pushed past her and took the phone from her hand. "Stop! Thief!" she shouted. The bus stopped, and the man jumped off and ran into a dark street.
Two passengers helped Mai and called the police. The police officers arrived quickly. They asked Mai what the thief looked like. "He was young and thin, and he had a red cap," she said.
The next day, the police watched video from a camera on the street. They saw the man clearly. Three days later, they arrested him in a market. He had taken five phones that week! He is now waiting to see a judge, and he may go to prison. Mai got her phone back. "Now I always keep my phone in my bag on the bus," she says.

Last month, our law class visited the city court to watch a real trial. The case was about a burglar who had broken into a jewellery shop at night. The suspect, a man in his thirties, said he was innocent.
First, the lawyer for the shop owner presented the evidence. Security cameras had filmed a man in a black hoodie entering the shop at 2 a.m., and his fingerprints were found on a broken window. Then a witness, a taxi driver, described seeing the man running down the street with a heavy bag.
The suspect's lawyer argued that the video was not clear and that the fingerprints could have been left earlier, when the man had visited the shop as a customer. The victim, the shop owner, looked very nervous when she answered questions.
In the end, the judge decided the man was guilty. His punishment was three years in prison. Our teacher explained that he could have received a longer sentence, but it was his first crime, and he had never tried to rob anyone before. It was fascinating to see how the law works in real life.

When a court reaches a guilty verdict, the next question is how the offender should be punished. In some countries, a jury of ordinary citizens decides whether someone is guilty, while a judge decides the sentence. Supporters of long prison sentences argue that harsh punishment acts as a deterrent: if people know they will spend years in jail, they will think twice before committing a crime.
Critics disagree. They point out that many people who are convicted of crimes such as vandalism or theft go on to reoffend after release. Prison, they argue, can teach young offenders more about crime than about honest work. Instead, they call for rehabilitation: education, job training and therapy that help prisoners return to society.
Modern technology has also changed how crimes are solved. Forensic science, such as DNA testing, means that a suspect's alibi can now be checked far more accurately. This has led to some innocent people being released after years in prison, and to more guilty people being successfully prosecuted.
Finally, experts warn that no justice system can work well where corruption exists. If police officers or officials accept a bribe, public trust disappears, and the law loses its power.
